title: An artificial muscle that can serve as the main actuator of a useful robot

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a manufacturable artificial muscle that provides the main joint motion of a useful, untethered robot. It would combine useful force, contraction, mechanical output, efficiency, response speed and durability while carrying the power supply and support equipment needed for ordinary work. Success would mean an integrated actuator system that repeatedly performs useful tasks, rather than a material that achieves one exceptional laboratory measurement.

Concept synthesis: skeletal muscle supplies a useful comparison across several dimensions—strain, stress, specific power, efficiency, bandwidth and cycle life—but matching a single biological benchmark would not establish this capability. The actuator must also work at sufficient size, connect effectively to the robot’s structure and remain controllable under load. The supplied evidence documents a related challenge for implantable artificial muscles; it does not establish whether the broader robotics goal remains unmet as of 1 November 2026.

significance.text: Conditional significance synthesis: combining compliant actuation with useful strength, motion, efficiency and durability could expand the range of robot limbs and body structures that engineers can build. Distributed muscle-like actuators could offer new ways to place force generation within a limb and accommodate contact during physical work. Human-scale strength would still require adequate actuator dimensions, load-bearing attachments and demonstrated integration; favorable performance per unit mass or volume does not guarantee a strong complete limb.

A related downstream possibility is augmenting or replacing biological muscle to restore function. Garrad and colleagues discuss this application while identifying substantial requirements beyond actuator performance: biomechanical interfaces, encapsulation, energy storage and transmission, and control. A successful robot actuator could therefore become a candidate technology for implants, but would not by itself establish implant safety, clinical effectiveness or suitability for long-term use in the body.

Impact synthesis: affordable consumer robots would additionally require economical production, consistent quality, maintainability and practical operating costs. Muscle-like actuation also would not automatically solve perception, dexterous control, reliable autonomy or energy storage. The biological analogy is useful for comparing a combination of capabilities, but it is neither a requirement to reproduce muscle’s mechanism nor a guarantee of animal-like overall performance.

missing_breakthrough.text: The proposed missing capability is one manufacturable actuator system that combines useful force and motion with efficient, responsive and durable operation as the primary actuator of an untethered robot. The strongest inspected evidence supplied here concerns implants: Garrad and colleagues identify simultaneous performance at the required physical scale, together with support-system integration, as key challenges. That finding supports the importance of coupled requirements without establishing a field-wide absence of useful robot muscles.

Engineering synthesis: the central challenge is preserving the combination of properties when moving from an actuator specimen to a working limb. Useful contraction must occur against the required load, at the required speed, and over repeated cycles. Its power source, drive electronics or pressure equipment, energy losses, attachments and control must fit within the robot’s mass and operating envelope. Manufacturability must then reproduce this performance consistently rather than depend on a specially prepared specimen.

The earlier research proposed general tradeoffs in which high work density comes with poor full-cycle efficiency, or high strain requires high voltage, pumping equipment or reduced force. These remain plausible issues to investigate, but the supplied review could not verify them as general rules across actuator classes. They should therefore be treated as candidate-specific questions to measure, rather than established universal barriers. The implant article provides firmer support for the broader need to meet multiple requirements and integrate supporting systems.

current_state.text: The supplied review identifies a complete three-page text of Garrad and colleagues’ “Performance metrics for implantable artificial muscles,” internally carrying DOI 10.1038/s44222-025-00400-8. Its prose gives mammalian muscle benchmarks of 0.60 MPa stress, 40 kJ/m³ work density and specific power as high as 280 W/kg. These are reference values reported by the article, not a demonstration that one artificial actuator simultaneously achieves them. The article discusses requirements for stress urinary incontinence and sit-to-stand assistance and states that meeting all implant performance targets at the necessary length scale remains challenging.

The research also attributes implant targets of 40% strain, 1.2 MPa stress, 60 kJ/m³ work density and 280 W/kg specific power at lengths of 50–300 mm to this article. The supplied review confirms the simultaneous-requirement discussion but does not independently confirm this complete numerical set or its allocation between the two clinical applications. Figure extraction was imperfect, so these numbers remain research-reported targets pending confirmation of their context. They are clinical estimates, not universal robotics thresholds. The research dates the article to 15 December 2025, whereas the retained PDF has a placeholder publication line; that exact date is not independently confirmed by the reviewed text.

The research identifies Mirvakili and Hunter’s “Artificial Muscles: Mechanisms, Applications, and Challenges” as first published on 18 December 2017 and describes an abstract-level survey of polymer, carbon-nanotube, shape-memory, dielectric, gel and pneumatic actuators. No inspectable artifact for that review was retained in the supplied evidence. Its class-by-class limitations and the inference that it identifies no drop-in robot muscle therefore cannot be verified here. Even a confirmed historical survey would not establish the field’s state in November 2026.

The research attributes to Hyeon and colleagues a Journal of Power Sources paper dated 1 August 2025 reporting coiled carbon-nanotube yarns with 6.1 J/g contractile work, described as approximately 152 times the maximum for human skeletal muscle, contractile efficiency up to 38.8% under one condition, and full-cycle efficiency of 6.7% when relaxation is included. The retained artifact contains only a redirect message, so the supplied review could verify neither the paper’s identity from that artifact nor these measurements, conditions or comparisons. The figures remain unverified research-reported results, not disproven results. As described, they concern actuator materials rather than an untethered robot limb. Contractile efficiency and full-cycle efficiency also have different boundaries and must not be treated as interchangeable or assumed to describe the same operating condition.

The research identifies Shi and Pikul’s “Achieving animal endurance in robots through advanced energy storage,” dated 30 April 2025, and attributes to it comparisons suggesting animal-like locomotion efficiency in bioinspired robots alongside a system-level energy-density deficit exceeding an order of magnitude because of batteries. The research access was limited to an abstract and a longer search extract, and no inspectable artifact was retained for review. These comparisons therefore remain unverified here. Their conceptual distinction remains useful: movement efficiency, stored energy and actuator performance describe different constraints, and improving endurance through energy storage would not by itself establish ROB-03.

Evidence-scope synthesis: the supplied materials document an implant-specific performance and integration challenge, alongside several incompletely verified historical and materials claims. They provide no bounded freshness search establishing coverage through 1 November 2026. Consequently, they establish neither achievement of the proposed robotics capability nor its continued absence across the field. Missing or inaccessible evidence limits the conclusion; it does not show that a reported result is false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed integrated demonstration: an untethered robot uses artificial muscles as its primary joint actuators and carries all required power and support systems. It operates without an external compressor or kilovolt tether, stands up under its own weight or lifts a specified grocery-scale load, walks several meters, and repeats a defined task sequence throughout a predefined work session without actuator replacement. Robot mass, payload, travel distance, session duration, repetitions and operating conditions should be specified before the demonstration. These are proposed criteria for this concept, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Primary artificial muscle joints complete an untethered robot work session

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement package: report strain, stress, force, displacement, mechanical work, specific power, response speed, cycle life and supply voltage or pressure under the conditions used for the robot task. State whether efficiencies cover contraction alone, a complete contraction–relaxation cycle, or the complete onboard system, including support equipment. Report actuator and support-system mass, energy consumption, degradation and failures. Where peak metrics require different loads or operating conditions, identify those differences instead of presenting the separate maxima as one simultaneous operating point.
completion_criteria.label: Robot task metrics reported with efficiency scope and separated peaks

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: repeat the demonstration across multiple manufactured actuators and robots, publish sufficient construction and testing detail for independent replication, and characterize the demonstrated load, speed, environmental and lifetime envelope. Report manufacturing variability, replacement needs and production assumptions. A successful finite test would establish useful capability within that envelope; it would not establish literal universality, indefinite lifetime or suitability for every robot.
completion_criteria.label: Repeated across manufactured units with replication detail and operating envelope

completion_criteria.text: Garrad and colleagues’ implant discussion motivates assessing simultaneous performance and support systems, but its clinical requirements do not prescribe the robot task above. An implant extension would require its own application-specific evaluation of size, biomechanical interfaces, encapsulation, energy delivery and control, followed by appropriate clinical validation. Passing a robot demonstration would not satisfy those additional requirements.
completion_criteria.label: Implant extension shown through its own evaluation and clinical validation

related_concepts.text: Roster comparison synthesis: ROB-01, “Reliable instruction-following physical work in unfamiliar everyday environments,” concerns dependable whole-robot behavior; ROB-02, “Autonomous dexterous tool use and in-hand manipulation at human reliability,” concerns manipulation reliability. ROB-03 could supply compliant, capable actuators for either, but actuator performance alone would not establish instruction following, perception, tool use or dexterity.

Roster comparison synthesis: ROB-07, “Predictive contact mechanics that plans real manipulation,” addresses anticipating physical interactions, while ROB-09, “Lifelong on-robot learning that retains and composes physical skills,” addresses acquiring and retaining behavior. Artificial-muscle dynamics would need to be represented in control and learning systems, but improved actuation would not by itself deliver predictive contact models or lifelong learning. Distributed tactile sensing is another complementary capability with a separate sensing objective.

Roster comparison synthesis: ROB-04, “Closed-loop robotic self-reproduction from feedstock,” requires a robot production loop; manufacturable artificial muscles could be one component of that loop. ROB-05, “Load-bearing robotic matter that reforms into working machines,” might incorporate distributed actuation, but additionally requires structural load bearing and reconfiguration. ROB-08, “Robot collectives that build functional structures from bulk material,” concerns coordinated construction. None follows directly from a successful muscle actuator, and none replaces ROB-03’s actuator-integration goal.

Roster comparison synthesis: ROB-06, “Untethered intervention at a target inside the living human body,” overlaps through compact actuation, onboard support and operation in a biological environment. ROB-10, “Completion of full surgical procedures on living patients,” could use compliant actuators within surgical equipment. Their respective goals are targeted intervention and complete surgical performance; neither is equivalent to restoring muscle function or demonstrating an artificial muscle as a robot’s primary actuator.

Cross-cutting synthesis: materials, power electronics, control and onboard energy storage all affect whether an artificial muscle becomes a useful robot actuator. Energy storage sets an important endurance boundary, while actuator efficiency determines part of the demand placed on it. These remain distinct engineering capabilities. Low-cost manufacture belongs within ROB-03’s practical deployment requirements, without requiring a separate concept or an unsupported historical claim about universal soft actuation.

unresolved_issues: Whether any actuator already satisfies the broader useful untethered robot goal as of 1 November 2026 remains unresolved; no bounded freshness search was supplied.

The Hyeon paper’s identity, numerical results, normalization basis, operating conditions and efficiency definitions require substantive source text; the retained artifact contains only a redirect message.
The Mirvakili–Hunter actuator-class descriptions and Shi–Pikul locomotion and energy-density comparisons lack inspectable artifacts in the supplied review.
The complete implant target set, its allocation between clinical applications and any dependence on imperfectly extracted figures remain unconfirmed by the supplied review.
The exact publication date of the Garrad article remains unresolved because the retained PDF uses a placeholder publication line.
Payload, work-session duration, repetition count, acceptable degradation and manufacturing scale remain to be chosen for an actual ROB-03 demonstration.

The review’s recommendation to withhold unverified performance numbers was not followed literally: the user requested preservation of quantitative detail when explicitly qualified, so the numbers remain clearly attributed research reports rather than verified achievements.

brief.title: Artificial muscles that power a working robot
possible: A robot could lift groceries, walk and repeat useful tasks using artificial muscles—devices that contract to move its joints. It would carry its own power supply and all supporting equipment.
The goal is a complete muscle system that manufacturers can reliably reproduce, with the strength, speed and working life needed for ordinary work.
why: Muscles that yield during contact could give engineers more ways to build robot limbs and place the parts that generate force throughout them. That could expand how robots move and handle physical work.
Related devices could eventually help people regain lost muscle function, including getting up from a chair. Restoring that movement could help people maintain mobility and independence.

sources.who: S. M. Mirvakili and I. W. Hunter
sources.showed: This review surveys artificial muscles made from different materials and driven by different mechanisms.
sources.cited_for: It provides background on approaches to artificial muscles.
sources.not_established: A survey does not demonstrate a muscle system powering a useful robot.

sources.who: Martin Garrad, Ross Burdis, Marcus Drake, Avril D. McCarthy and Jonathan Rossiter
sources.showed: They estimated what implanted muscles would need to restore bladder control or help someone stand. Existing devices can meet individual performance targets, but combining them at the required size remains a challenge.
sources.quote:
forces of 2.7 N may be 
sufficient to prevent urinary leakage at rest
sources.cited_for: Useful artificial muscles must combine performance at a practical size with power, control and reliable attachments.
sources.not_established: The analysis does not demonstrate a working robot muscle or a clinically validated implant.

sources.showed: This is a study of contraction and energy efficiency in coiled yarns made from tiny carbon tubes.
sources.cited_for: It concerns muscle material performance and the distinction between contraction efficiency and efficiency over a complete cycle.
sources.not_established: Material measurements do not establish performance in a robot carrying its own power and supporting equipment.

sources.showed: This work examines robot endurance through comparisons of movement efficiency and energy storage.
sources.cited_for: Stored energy and movement efficiency impose separate limits on robot endurance.
sources.not_established: Better energy storage alone does not establish a useful artificial muscle system.

shown: Garrad and colleagues describe artificial muscles that meet individual targets for implants. Combining those targets at the size needed for use in the body remains difficult. Hyeon and colleagues report contraction in coiled carbon yarns, a material result rather than a working robot limb.
missing: A robot must complete useful work with artificial muscles driving its main joints and all power and support equipment onboard.
The complete system must combine useful strength and movement with efficient, responsive operation that survives repeated use.
Manufacturing must reproduce that performance consistently across devices, with reliable attachments and control under load.

milestones.label: A robot completes work using onboard artificial muscles
milestones.explanation: A robot would have to carry all equipment, stand or lift a defined load, walk and repeat tasks through a defined session without muscle replacement. This would establish useful operation as a complete system.

milestones.label: Task measurements reveal the complete system's performance
milestones.explanation: Measurements would have to cover movement, force, work, speed, lifetime, energy use and equipment weight, separating efficiency scopes and peaks under different conditions. This would establish what the robot achieves together.

milestones.label: Manufactured devices repeat the result within known limits
milestones.explanation: Multiple manufactured muscles and robots would have to repeat the task, with enough detail for independent reproduction and known operating limits. This would establish consistency and practical boundaries.

milestones.label: An implant passes its own clinical evaluation
milestones.explanation: An implant would need separate evaluation of size, tissue attachments, protective covering, power and control, followed by clinical validation. This would establish suitability for restoring function in the body.

uncertain: Whether an existing artificial muscle system already meets the broader robot goal remains unresolved.
The required payload, session length, repetitions, acceptable wear and production scale remain to be chosen.
Each candidate needs measurements that distinguish energy used during contraction from energy used over a complete cycle and by supporting equipment.

page.title: Artificial-muscle actuation for untethered robots
page.definition: Manufactured artificial muscles—devices that contract when stimulated—provide a robot’s main joint motion. The robot carries its energy source and supporting equipment and repeatedly performs a specified work task in its intended operating environment.

goal.need: A carbon-nanotube-yarn study reports maxima of 38.8% contraction-only efficiency and 6.7% full-cycle efficiency under different conditions. These quantities exclude the additional equipment required by a robot. An untethered fluidic quadruped therefore required actuator design around its onboard pneumatic supply, limited to 0.24 MPa. The system must combine contraction, energy conversion and supporting equipment within the robot’s operating requirements.

completion.title: An artificial-muscle robot routinely performs its specified work task with all supporting equipment onboard.
completion.criterion: A robot is deployed and routinely completes a specified work task in its intended environment. Artificial muscles provide its main joint motion; its energy source, drive electronics, pressure source where needed, cooling and controls are onboard. It meets the application’s published load, duty-cycle and service-life acceptance requirements. Muscle units made by the specified manufacturing process meet those requirements when installed. No universal payload, operating duration, lifetime or production volume is prescribed.
completion.set_by: Atlas; application-specific operational endpoint informed by NOAA’s Level 9 readiness definition.
completion.basis: Searches of ONR MURI, EIC project objectives, ISO/ASTM websites, NASA EAP challenge descriptions and developer roadmaps found no combined acceptance test covering robot work, onboard support, durability and manufacture. NOAA defines Level 9 through routine deployment; the European Commission distinguishes qualification from operational proof. This endpoint applies that distinction to the capability defined here. The cited prototype results do not establish completion.

milestones.title: An artificial-muscle specimen produces mechanical work against a load in an experimental proof of concept.
milestones.criterion: A stimulated artificial-muscle specimen contracts against a load and produces mechanical work, satisfying experimental proof of concept, TRL 3. An electrochemical example published on 1 August 2025 reports 6.1 J/g contractile work and 13.1% contraction-only efficiency with tetrabutylammonium ions; its accessible abstract supplies no specimen count. The fluidic, electrostatic and thermal robot demonstrations cited at the next milestone also establish working actuators.
milestones.set_by: European Commission, EU Funding & Tenders Online Manual, TRL 3. This is a generic technology-readiness criterion applied to artificial muscles, not a muscle-specific performance target.

milestones.title: An artificial-muscle drive is validated in an integrated laboratory robot.
milestones.criterion: The drive operates as an integrated robot subsystem in the laboratory, corresponding to TRL 4. Fluidic: a 794 g quadruped walked untethered at 0.16 body-lengths/s, published on 27 March 2026. Electrostatic: the HALVE swimmer reached 3.8 cm/s in tap water at 2 Hz in the preprint revised on 30 August 2023, subsequently published in Science Advances. Thermal: the 88 mg RoBeetle carried up to 230 mg, published on 19 August 2020. These are prototype results, not formal TRL assessments; independent robot counts were not established.
milestones.set_by: European Commission, EU Funding & Tenders Online Manual, TRL 4. The laboratory-validation criterion is generic.

milestones.title: An artificial-muscle robot prototype demonstrates its intended task in its operational environment.
milestones.criterion: An integrated prototype demonstrates the intended work task in its operational environment, corresponding to TRL 7. The RoBeetle paper reports thermal-muscle locomotion outdoors on concrete, but does not establish deployment for an operational service task. The cited fluidic quadruped and electrostatic swimmer demonstrate laboratory operation. No corresponding operational-task demonstration was located for the electrochemical case.
milestones.set_by: European Commission, EU Funding & Tenders Online Manual, TRL 7. The operational-environment criterion is generic.
milestones.threshold_quote: system prototype demonstration in operational environment

milestones.title: The complete artificial-muscle robot is qualified for its specified application.
milestones.criterion: The final robot system, including its artificial-muscle drive and onboard supporting equipment, is complete and qualified against its application requirements, corresponding to TRL 8. Qualification precedes routine operational use. The cited actuator and prototype publications do not establish qualification of such a complete system for any listed mechanism. The Commission’s definition supplies no universal numerical requirement for force, efficiency, lifetime or manufacturing volume.
milestones.set_by: European Commission, EU Funding & Tenders Online Manual, TRL 8. This is a generic qualification stage, not certification of an artificial-muscle product.

not_found: No artificial-muscle-specific acceptance test combining operational work, onboard support, durability and manufacturing repeatability was found.
No publication establishing complete-system qualification or routine operational use under the completion test was located for the four listed mechanisms.
No electrochemical artificial-muscle robot integration demonstration was located in the sources searched.
Independent specimen counts for the yarn efficiency measurements and independent robot counts for the cited demonstrations could not be established from the accessible texts.
NASA’s EAP arm-wrestling rules returned access errors; no threshold from those rules is used.

results.finding: Peano-HASEL electrostatic actuator, specimen count not stated, achieved 63.6% closed-cycle efficiency while producing mechanical work.
results.detail: The actuator had seven pouches. Peak efficiency occurred at 7 kV, 30 N and 0.25 Hz. The measurement assumes charge recovery and excludes corona losses to the environment on the high-voltage side.
results.quote: For our cycle, the maximum efficiency of 63.6% occurred at a prescribed peak voltage of 7 kV and a prescribed peak force of 30 N.

results.finding: Thermally actuated coiled nylon 6,6 muscle produced 2.48 kJ/kg of contractile work; specimen count not stated.
results.detail: The muscle contracted against an applied load during thermal actuation.
results.quote:
The
maximum specific work during contraction was
2.48 kJ/kg for the C= 1.1 nylon 6,6 muscle of
Fig. 2C ( 1), which is 64 times that for natural
muscle (19).

results.finding: Electrochemical CNT yarn muscle (specimen count not stated) achieved 270 J/kg of contractile work.
results.detail: During a full voltage-scanning cycle, maximum work capacity was reached under 53 MPa of applied tension.
results.quote:
In contrast, the work capa-
city increased with stress, reaching a maximum of 270 J kg−1 at 53 MPa,
approximately 6.7 times higher than that of mammalian skeletal
muscle (40 J kg−1)30.

results.finding: One HALVE-actuated robotic fish reached a maximum swimming speed of 3.8 cm/s.
results.detail: The fully untethered swimmer operated in room-temperature tap water with antagonistic actuation at 2 Hz. The number of independent robots was not established.
results.quote:
We observed a maximum swimming velocity of 3.8 cm s
−1
, equivalent to 0.14 body length/s at 2-Hz antagonistic actuation.

results.finding: An electrochemical muscle lifted a bionic arm by 5 mm; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The laboratory arm demonstrates muscle-driven motion, but the text does not establish an untethered robot with onboard energy and support equipment or repeated task performance.
